comparison: Both evaluations support the core finding that human Aβ42 inhibits γ-secretase in cell-free systems (C3, C22-C28). OpenEval provides detailed analysis of dose-response, substrate dependence, and reversibility data across claims C3-C36, while peer review focuses on the biochemical assay findings (C3, C22-C28) and explicitly states the data are 'convincing.' Both agree the evidence is strong.

OpenEval R1 includes mechanistic claims about reversibility and non-substrate behavior (C29-C36), while peer R3 evaluates these same claims. Both evaluations support the mechanistic interpretation. Peer review implicitly accepts these findings as part of the 'convincing' overall evidence without raising specific concerns.

Both evaluations support the structure-activity relationship findings showing specificity of human Aβ42 over murine Aβ42 and truncated variants (C37-C46). OpenEval provides detailed analysis of the SAR data, while peer review implicitly accepts the specificity through their statement that human Aβ42 'convincingly' inhibits γ-secretase, which encompasses the negative controls (C4, C5, C37-C46).

Both evaluations support the cellular validation experiments showing APP-CTF accumulation and reduced Aβ secretion across multiple cell types (C47-C53). OpenEval emphasizes the consistency across cell types and lack of cytotoxicity, while peer review accepts these findings as part of the convincing overall evidence without raising methodological concerns.

OpenEval R3 includes claims about cellular specificity (C54-C55) that overlap with peer R5's evaluation of differential uptake and specificity (C54-C55, C57-C59). Both evaluations support these findings. The evaluations address overlapping aspects of why only human Aβ42 shows cellular effects.

Both evaluations support the differential cellular uptake findings (C57-C59) that explain why only human Aβ42 shows cellular inhibitory effects. OpenEval emphasizes the endolysosomal accumulation pattern, while peer review implicitly accepts this mechanistic explanation as part of the overall convincing evidence for specificity.

Perfect alignment on FRET biosensor data (C60-C61). Both evaluations support this orthogonal validation of γ-secretase inhibition in living neurons. OpenEval explicitly notes this as independent confirmation, while peer review implicitly accepts it as part of the convincing evidence without raising concerns.

Perfect alignment on mechanistic dissection experiments (C62-C70). Both evaluations support the exclusion of alternative mechanisms and accept that γ-secretase inhibition is the primary effect. OpenEval notes the additional mechanisms suggested by time-zero data, while peer review accepts the overall mechanistic interpretation without challenge.

Perfect alignment on conditioned medium experiments (C71-C73, C93). Both evaluations support the finding that biologically-derived Aβ is more potent than recombinant peptides at physiologically relevant concentrations. Neither evaluation raises concerns about methodology or interpretation.

Perfect alignment on broad substrate inhibition data (C74-C80). Both evaluations support the finding that Aβ42 inhibits multiple γ-secretase substrates. OpenEval emphasizes the competitive mechanism and substrate-independence, while peer review accepts the broad impact as having implications beyond APP processing.

Both evaluations support the functional consequences of γ-secretase inhibition in p75/TrkA-dependent cell death (C84-C88). OpenEval provides detailed analysis of the TrkA-dependence validating the mechanism, while peer review implicitly accepts these functional data as part of the convincing overall findings.

Perfect alignment on human tissue data showing physiologically relevant Aβ42 concentrations in AD synaptosomes (C89-C91). Both evaluations support the translational relevance. OpenEval notes the caveat about volume estimation, while peer review accepts the findings as demonstrating disease relevance.

Perfect alignment on the proposed mechanistic model (C8, C94, C96-C98). OpenEval rates this as UNCERTAIN due to speculative elements requiring validation, while peer review rates it as SUPPORTED, accepting the framework as reasonable interpretation. This represents a subtle difference in evaluation stringency for speculative claims, though both acknowledge the model's consistency with data.

OpenEval R12 evaluates background/context claims (C1-C21) establishing scientific context through literature citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found. These are appropriately cited background claims that OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED.
OpenEval R13 evaluates citations to prior work (C32, C40, C45) referencing Szaruga et al. 2017. No corresponding peer review evaluation found. OpenEval rates these contextual citations as SUPPORTED.

OpenEval R14 evaluates explicitly speculative claims about AD pathogenesis and FAD mechanisms (C92, C103-C104, C109-C113). OpenEval rates these as UNCERTAIN requiring validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found that specifically addresses these speculative hypotheses.

OpenEval R15 evaluates discussion-related literature citations (C95, C99-C102, C105-C108) contextualizing broader implications. OpenEval rates these as SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific contextual citations.
